abstract.text:
For sophisticated reinforcement learning (RL) systems to interact usefully with
real-world environments, we need to communicate complex goals to these systems.
In this work, we explore goals defined in terms of (non-expert) human preferences
between pairs of trajectory segments. We show that this approach can effectively
solve complex RL tasks without access to the reward function, including Atari
games and simulated robot locomotion, while providing feedback on less than
1% of our agent’s interactions with the environment. This reduces the cost of
human oversight far enough that it can be practically applied to state-of-the-art
RL systems. To demonstrate the flexibility of our approach, we show that we can
successfully train complex novel behaviors with about an hour of human time.
These behaviors and environments are considerably more complex than any which
have been previously learned from human feedback.

source_span.end_text: Our algorithm fits a reward function to the human’s preferences while simultaneously training a policy to optimize the current predicted reward function
source_span.start_text: For sophisticated reinforcement learning (RL) systems to interact usefully with real-world environments, we need to communicate complex goals to these systems.

sections.summary: The paper motivates learning from human preferences for deep RL when reward functions are hard to specify. It proposes fitting a reward model to pairwise preference comparisons over short trajectory clips and optimizing a policy against that learned reward. It previews Atari and simulated robot locomotion results with very sparse feedback and novel behaviors learned in about an hour.
sections.title: Motivation and Contributions

source_span.end_text: Compared to all prior work, our key contribution is to scale human feedback up to deep reinforcement learning and to learn much more complex behaviors.
source_span.start_text: A long line of work studies reinforcement learning from human ratings or rankings

sections.summary: Positions the work against prior preference-based RL, trajectory preference queries, and interactive human-reward methods. It argues the key advance is scaling human feedback to deep RL and complex behaviors, using nonlinear reward models, asynchronous training, and ensembling.
sections.title: Related Work and Positioning

source_span.end_text: Our model based on trajectory segment comparisons is very similar to the trajectory preference queries used in Wilson et al. (2012), except that we don’t assume that we can reset the system to an arbitrary state² and so our segments generally begin from different states.
source_span.start_text: Instead of assuming that the environment produces a reward signal, we assume that there is a human overseer who can express preferences between trajectory segments.

sections.summary: Formalizes the setting: an agent interacts with an environment, but instead of receiving a reward signal it receives human preferences over trajectory segments. Evaluation can be quantitative when preferences are generated by a reward function, or qualitative when only natural-language goals are available.
sections.title: Problem Setting and Evaluation Goals

source_span.end_text: We decide how to query preferences based on an approximation to the uncertainty in the reward function estimator, similar to Daniel et al. (2014)
source_span.start_text: At each point in time our method maintains a policy π: O → A and a reward function estimate r̂: O × A → R, each parametrized by deep neural networks.

sections.summary: Describes the asynchronous method: a policy interacts with the environment, pairs of trajectory clips are sent to a human for comparison, and a reward predictor is trained on those comparisons. Reward fitting uses a Bradley-Terry-style cross-entropy loss, with ensembling, validation, regularization, a random-response correction, and uncertainty-based query selection.
sections.title: Method: Learning a Reward Model from Preferences

source_span.end_text: Real human feedback is typically only slightly less effective than the synthetic feedback; depending on the task human feedback ranged from being half as efficient as ground truth feedback to being equally efficient.
source_span.start_text: We implemented our algorithm in TensorFlow (Abadi et al., 2016).

sections.summary: Reports the experimental setup and simulated robotics results. With 700 human labels, the method nearly matches RL using the true reward across MuJoCo tasks; learned reward models are less stable and higher variance, and human feedback is usually slightly less effective than synthetic feedback but can outperform it via useful shaping.
sections.title: Experimental Setup and Simulated Robotics Results

source_span.end_text: On Qbert, our method fails to learn to beat the first level with real human feedback; this may be because short clips in Qbert can be confusing and difficult to evaluate.
source_span.start_text: The second set of tasks we consider is a set of seven Atari games in the Arcade Learning Environment (Bellemare et al., 2013), the same games presented in Mnih et al., 2013.

sections.summary: Evaluates the method on seven Atari games with 5,500 human queries and synthetic labels. It learns substantially but often does not fully match RL; performance is strong on BeamRider and Pong, slower on Seaquest and Qbert, and improved but sub-RL on SpaceInvaders and Breakout. Human feedback is similar to or slightly worse than synthetic feedback, with Qbert and Enduro highlighting labeling and shaping issues.
sections.title: Atari Results

source_span.end_text: Keeping alongside other cars in Enduro. This was trained with roughly 1,300 queries and 4 million frames of interaction with the environment
source_span.start_text: Using the same parameters as in the previous experiments, we show that our algorithm can learn novel complex behaviors.

sections.summary: Demonstrates that the same method can learn novel behaviors without an explicit reward function. Examples include Hopper backflips, Half-Cheetah forward movement on one leg, and Enduro staying alongside other cars; these required hundreds to about 1,300 queries and roughly under an hour to a few hours of feedback.
sections.title: Novel Behaviors from Human Preferences

source_span.end_text: In general we discovered that asking humans to compare longer clips was significantly more helpful per clip, and significantly less helpful per frame.
source_span.start_text: In order to better understand the performance of our algorithm, we consider a range of modifications:

sections.summary: Ablates query selection, ensembling, online versus offline labels, regularization, segment length, and target regression. Offline reward training fails because the predictor captures only part of a nonstationary reward; comparisons beat absolute scores for continuous control; and longer clips are better per clip but worse per frame.
sections.title: Ablation Studies and Design Insights

source_span.end_text: In the long run it would be desirable to make learning a task from human preferences no more difficult than learning it from a programmatic reward signal
source_span.start_text: Agent-environment interactions are often radically cheaper than human interaction.

sections.summary: Concludes that supervised reward learning from human preferences can reduce interaction complexity by roughly three orders of magnitude, making preference-based deep RL economically plausible. It frames the work as the first evidence that these techniques scale to state-of-the-art RL and calls for future work on efficiency, task range, and long-term alignment with complex human values.
sections.title: Discussion and Conclusions

source_span.end_text: Christian Wirth, J Fürnkranz, Gerhard Neumann, et al. Model-free preference-based reinforcement learning. In AAAI, pages 2222–2228, 2016.
source_span.start_text: We thank Olivier Pietquin, Bilal Piot, Laurent Orseau, Pedro Ortega, Victoria Krakovna, Owain Evans, Andrej Karpathy, Igor Mordatch, and Jack Clark for reading drafts of the paper.

sections.summary: Navigation-only unit containing the acknowledgments and the paper’s bibliography. It does not add substantive argument beyond crediting readers, contractors, and institutions and listing references.
sections.title: Acknowledgments and References

source_span.end_text: For the reward predictor, we use 84x84 images as inputs (the same as the inputs to the policy), and stack 4 frames for a total 84x84x4 input tensor.
source_span.start_text: Many RL environments have termination conditions that depend on the behavior of the agent, such as ending an episode when the agent dies or falls over.

sections.summary: Documents experimental details: removal of variable-length episodes to avoid leaking task information, MuJoCo TRPO settings and reward-predictor architecture, label schedules, and Atari wrappers and A2C hyperparameters. It also specifies the convolutional reward predictor and pretraining/label-annealing procedure.
sections.title: Appendix A: Experimental Details

source_span.end_text: Don’t worry about how the agent got into the situation it is in (for instance, it doesn’t matter if one agent has more lives, or is now on a more advanced level); just focus on what happens in the clip itself.
source_span.start_text: Look at the clips and select the one in which better things happen. Only decide on events you actually witness in the clip.

sections.summary: Provides the exact instructions given to human contractors for MuJoCo and Atari. It defines good and bad behavior per domain or game, explains tie and “can’t tell” choices, gives keyboard shortcuts and FAQ answers, and emphasizes judging only what happens in the clip.
sections.title: Appendix B: Contractor Instructions

source_span.end_text: Our algorithm fits a reward function to the human’s preferences while simultaneously training a policy to optimize the current predicted reward function
source_span.start_text: For sophisticated reinforcement learning (RL) systems to interact usefully with real-world environments, we need to communicate complex goals to these systems.

sections.summary: The paper motivates learning from human preferences for deep RL when reward functions are hard to specify. It proposes fitting a reward model to pairwise preference comparisons over short trajectory clips and optimizing a policy against that learned reward. It previews Atari and simulated robot locomotion results with very sparse feedback and novel behaviors learned in about an hour.
sections.title: Motivation and Contributions

source_span.end_text: Compared to all prior work, our key contribution is to scale human feedback up to deep reinforcement learning and to learn much more complex behaviors.
source_span.start_text: A long line of work studies reinforcement learning from human ratings or rankings

sections.summary: Positions the work against prior preference-based RL, trajectory preference queries, and interactive human-reward methods. It argues the key advance is scaling human feedback to deep RL and complex behaviors, using nonlinear reward models, asynchronous training, and ensembling.
sections.title: Related Work and Positioning

source_span.end_text: Our model based on trajectory segment comparisons is very similar to the trajectory preference queries used in Wilson et al. (2012), except that we don’t assume that we can reset the system to an arbitrary state² and so our segments generally begin from different states.
source_span.start_text: Instead of assuming that the environment produces a reward signal, we assume that there is a human overseer who can express preferences between trajectory segments.

sections.summary: Formalizes the setting: an agent interacts with an environment, but instead of receiving a reward signal it receives human preferences over trajectory segments. Evaluation can be quantitative when preferences are generated by a reward function, or qualitative when only natural-language goals are available.
sections.title: Problem Setting and Evaluation Goals

source_span.end_text: We decide how to query preferences based on an approximation to the uncertainty in the reward function estimator, similar to Daniel et al. (2014)
source_span.start_text: At each point in time our method maintains a policy π: O → A and a reward function estimate r̂: O × A → R, each parametrized by deep neural networks.

sections.summary: Describes the asynchronous method: a policy interacts with the environment, pairs of trajectory clips are sent to a human for comparison, and a reward predictor is trained on those comparisons. Reward fitting uses a Bradley-Terry-style cross-entropy loss, with ensembling, validation, regularization, a random-response correction, and uncertainty-based query selection.

sections.summary: Reports the experimental setup and simulated robotics results. With 700 human labels, the method nearly matches RL using the true reward across MuJoCo tasks; learned reward models are less stable and higher variance, and human feedback is usually slightly less effective than synthetic feedback but can outperform it via useful shaping.

sections.summary: Evaluates the method on seven Atari games with 5,500 human queries and synthetic labels. It learns substantially but often does not fully match RL; performance is strong on BeamRider and Pong, slower on Seaquest and Qbert, and improved but sub-RL on SpaceInvaders and Breakout. Human feedback is similar to or slightly worse than synthetic feedback, with Qbert and Enduro highlighting labeling and shaping issues.

source_span.start_text: Using the same parameters as in the previous experiments, we show that our algorithm can learn novel complex behaviors.

sections.summary: Demonstrates that the same method can learn novel behaviors without an explicit reward function. Examples include Hopper backflips, Half-Cheetah forward movement on one leg, and Enduro staying alongside other cars; these required hundreds to about 1,300 queries and roughly under an hour to a few hours of feedback.
sections.title: Novel Behaviors from Human Preferences

source_span.end_text: In general we discovered that asking humans to compare longer clips was significantly more helpful per clip, and significantly less helpful per frame.

sections.summary: Ablates query selection, ensembling, online versus offline labels, regularization, segment length, and target regression. Offline reward training fails because the predictor captures only part of a nonstationary reward; comparisons beat absolute scores for continuous control; and longer clips are better per clip but worse per frame.
sections.title: Ablation Studies and Design Insights

source_span.end_text: In the long run it would be desirable to make learning a task from human preferences no more difficult than learning it from a programmatic reward signal
source_span.start_text: Agent-environment interactions are often radically cheaper than human interaction.

sections.summary: Concludes that supervised reward learning from human preferences can reduce interaction complexity by roughly three orders of magnitude, making preference-based deep RL economically plausible. It frames the work as the first evidence that these techniques scale to state-of-the-art RL and calls for future work on efficiency, task range, and long-term alignment with complex human values.
